fields.Front: Write the final case-study schema with all keys and foreign keys.
fields.Back:
EMPLOYEE (SSN, Fname, Minit, Lname, Address, Salary, Sex, Birthdate, SuperSSN (FK->EMPLOYEE), DNumber (FK->DEPARTMENT))
DEPARTMENT (DNumber, DName, MgrSSN (FK->EMPLOYEE), MgrStartDate)
DEPT_LOCATIONS (DNumber (FK), Location) PK (DNumber, Location)
PROJECT (PNumber, PName, PLocation, DNumber (FK->DEPARTMENT))
WORKS_ON (ESSN (FK), PNumber (FK), Hours) PK (ESSN, PNumber)
DEPENDENT (ESSN (FK), DependentName, Sex, Birthdate, Relationship) PK (ESSN, DependentName)

fields.Front: Case study: why does DEPARTMENT hold the manager, and what does step 3 add?
fields.Back: MANAGES is 1:1 and DEPARTMENT has TOTAL participation (every department has a manager, but most employees manage nothing), so by step 3 the key moves from the partial side into the total side: DEPARTMENT gains MgrSSN (FK to EMPLOYEE) and MgrStartDate, the relationship's attribute.

fields.Front: Case study: which three columns does step 4 add, and why is DEPENDENTS_OF not mapped again?
fields.Back: EMPLOYEE gets the department number from WORKS FOR and the supervisor's SSN from the unary SUPERVISES; PROJECT gets the managing department number from CONTROLS. DEPENDENTS_OF is not mapped again because step 2 already handled it: the weak entity DEPENDENT took the owner's SSN as a foreign key that is part of its key.

fields.Front: Case study: how is the unary SUPERVISES mapped, and why is Borg's SuperSSN null?
fields.Back: As a foreign key SuperSSN in EMPLOYEE that references EMPLOYEE's OWN primary key SSN (step 4). Borg's SuperSSN is NULL because he is the top of the hierarchy: SUPERVISES is partial on the supervisee side, and a foreign key from a partial relationship may be null.

fields.Front: Case study: why can two dependents both be named Alice, and why is Location left out of DEPARTMENT?
fields.Back: DEPENDENT's key is (ESSN, DependentName), so the same name under different employees is distinct - only the composite key tells the two Alices apart. Location is MULTI-VALUED, so rule 6 says not to make it an attribute of DEPARTMENT; it gets its own table DEPT_LOCATIONS keyed by (DNumber, Location).

fields.Front: What steps does the instructor take in Access to create a table, and what happens when you mark the primary key?
fields.Back: In table Design View add each column with its data type, then select the key column(s) and press the PRIMARY KEY button before saving. 'Notice when we make it the key, it is now a REQUIRED field' - Required turns to Yes, so the key must always be entered. Then save with a meaningful name: 'Table1 is a very bad name, so don't call it Table1; call it Project.'

fields.Front: What data types does the instructor choose in Access for SSN, Birthdate and Salary, and what mistake does she admit?
fields.Back: SSN: Number (or Short Text, 'because you're not really doing calculations with it'); Birthdate: Date; Salary: Currency. Her admitted mistake: she stored the whole name in ONE column, when step 1 says a composite attribute should be split into first-name and last-name columns.

fields.Front: How do you create a relationship in the Access Relationships window?
fields.Back: Database Tools -> Relationships; add all the tables and arrange them like the ER diagram; for each foreign key DRAG the primary key onto the foreign key column; tick ENFORCE REFERENTIAL INTEGRITY; click Create. Access reports the relationship as one-to-many, and 'lets us draw a little mini version of the ER diagram'.

fields.Front: How does Access display the unary SUPERVISES relationship, and how is the M:N relationship drawn?
fields.Back: Access shows a SECOND COPY of EMPLOYEE to draw the line from SSN to SupervisorSSN, 'but these are still really both the same table'. The M:N is drawn as two relationships into the linking table: EMPLOYEE.SSN onto WORKS_ON.ESSN and PROJECT.PNumber onto WORKS_ON.PNumber - 'together this becomes a many-to-many relationship'.

fields.Front: List the practical Access habits the instructor says will save you marks.
fields.Back:
1. Name every table sensibly - never Table1
2. Set the primary key BEFORE saving, so the DBMS marks it Required
3. For composite keys, select all the key columns together before pressing Primary Key
4. Give every foreign key the SAME data type as the primary key it references
5. Do not create a column for a multi-valued attribute in the entity's own table
6. Do not map a weak entity's identifying relationship a second time in step 4

fields.Front: APPLICATION: reading the case-study ER diagram aloud, which rule does each sentence trigger?
fields.Back:
'An employee has many dependents; DEPENDENT is weak' -> step 2.
'An employee works on many projects, with Hours' -> step 5.
'A department has many employees' -> step 4.
'A department is managed by one employee, with StartDate' -> step 3.
'An employee supervises many employees' (unary) -> step 4.
'A department controls many projects' -> step 4.
'A department has several locations' -> step 6.

fields.Text: Mapping the case-study ER diagram gives six tables: {{c1::EMPLOYEE}}, {{c1::DEPARTMENT}}, {{c1::DEPT_LOCATIONS}}, PROJECT, WORKS_ON and DEPENDENT.

A foreign key column must have the {{c1::same data type}} as the key it references (if DNumber is a Number in DEPARTMENT it must be a Number in DEPT_LOCATIONS); to make a composite primary key in Access you {{c1::highlight all the key columns together}} and click Primary Key.
In the case study, step {{c1::6}} needed no extra work (DEPT_LOCATIONS was built right after DEPARTMENT) and step {{c1::7}} did not apply, because there are {{c1::no ternary relationships}}.

Case-study keys: WORKS_ON has primary key {{c1::(ESSN, PNumber)}} (step 5); DEPENDENT has {{c1::(ESSN, DependentName)}} (step 2); DEPT_LOCATIONS has {{c1::(DNumber, Location)}} (step 6); EMPLOYEE carries the foreign keys SuperSSN and DNumber (step 4).

In Access, marking a column as the primary key makes it a {{c1::Required}} field; a new table must not be left named {{c1::Table1}}; and a relationship is created by dragging the {{c1::primary key}} onto the foreign key column and ticking Enforce Referential Integrity.

Textbook (Elmasri Table 9.1): ER to relational - an entity type gives an {{c1::entity relation}}; an M:N relationship type gives a {{c1::relationship relation and two foreign keys}}; a composite attribute gives a set of simple component attributes; a multivalued attribute gives {{c1::a relation and a foreign key}}; a value set gives a domain; a key attribute gives a primary or secondary key.
